summary: Stateful PCE extensions let a PCE control MPLS traffic engineering paths that clients already have. This document extends PCEP so a PCE can itself start the setup of a new label switched path, instead of only reacting to a client's request.

eli5.summary: Usually the driver asks the map app for a route. Here the map app can say, set up this route, and the road system does it.

subtitle: Lets a central path computation server tell a router to build and tear down label switched paths on demand.

tldr.problem: Stateful PCE extensions let a PCE control paths that were already configured on the router, which suits static networks but not ones where paths must be created and removed as applications ask for them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8281 adds a PCInitiate message that a PCE sends to a PCC to create or delete an LSP, plus an I capability flag, an R flag in the SRP object and a C flag in the LSP object. The PCC sets the LSP up with RSVP-TE and delegates it to the PCE.
tldr.outcome: A controller can create, update and remove LSPs on demand without any local configuration on the router, with limits and timers to protect both sides. It is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 8281 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: From Delegated LSPs to PCE-Initiated LSPs
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a Path Computation Element (PCE) talk about computing MPLS Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths (TE LSPs). RFC 8231 added stateful control: LSPs are configured on the PCC, and the PCC delegates control of them to the PCE.

This document goes one step further. It describes the setup, maintenance and teardown of PCE-initiated LSPs, meaning LSPs that are instantiated as a result of a request from the PCE, without any local configuration on the PCC. The goal is a dynamic network that is centrally controlled and deployed.
sections.eli5: Before, the router already knew about its roads and just asked the helper for advice. Now the helper can tell the router to build a brand new road.

sections.title: Why a PCE Would Start an LSP
sections.content:
The model in RFC 8231 relies on the Label Edge Router taking an active role in delegating locally configured LSPs. That works well where LSP placement is fairly static. Where placement must change in response to application demands, it is useful to create and tear down LSPs dynamically, and a PCE that can trigger creation on demand fits into a controller-based network architecture.

The RFC gives three use cases:

  • A software-defined network where an application asks the PCE for a path with certain constraints between two Label Switching Routers. The PCE computes it and instructs the head end LSR to instantiate and signal it, and later requests its teardown.
  • Adjusting aggregate bandwidth between two points with multiple LSPs, similar to auto-bandwidth. This avoids two limits of auto-bandwidth: growing capacity beyond the capacity of individual links, and poor bin packing.
  • Demand engineering, where a PCE that sees both network state and the demand matrix creates new paths to optimize traffic distribution.
sections.eli5: If a town needs a new road only some days, it is better to build and remove it when needed than to keep every possible road open forever.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
A PCEP speaker announces support during session setup. The STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV in the Open message gains a new I flag (LSP-INSTANTIATION-CAPABILITY). A PCC sets it to say it allows instantiation by a PCE, and a PCE sets it to say it supports instantiating LSPs. Both sides must set it. A PCE can initiate LSPs only for PCCs that advertised the capability.

To create an LSP, the PCE sends a PCInitiate message. The PCC creates the LSP from the attributes the PCE gave, using local values for anything unspecified, and then sends a PCRpt report that carries a newly assigned PLSP-ID and delegates the LSP to the PCE through the Delegate flag. Later changes use PCUpd messages, and both sides then use the PCC-assigned PLSP-ID. Deleting uses PCInitiate with the R flag set, and the PCC answers with a PCRpt for the removed state. When to create or delete is outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: The helper and the router first agree that they both know this game. Then the helper says build it, the router builds it and says done, and later the helper says remove it.

sections.title: The PCInitiate Message and Its Flags
sections.content:
The PCInitiate message has Message-Type 12. It MUST include the SRP and LSP objects and MAY contain others. A list of requests can be carried in one message, and each is either an instantiation (SRP, LSP, optional END-POINTS, ERO and optional attributes) or a deletion (just SRP and LSP).

The SRP object carries an SRP-ID-number that is unique within a PCEP session. The PCE increments the last-used value before each PCInitiate, and the PCC MUST echo it in the PCErr and PCRpt messages it sends as a result, so the PCE can match replies to requests. The new R flag (LSP-REMOVE) in the SRP object is 0 for create and 1 for remove.

The LSP object gains a C flag (Create). On a PCRpt, C set to 1 means the LSP was created by a PCInitiate message, and it MUST be 1 on each PCRpt for the LSP's whole existence. This lets PCEs know which LSPs were PCE initiated. The optional SPEAKER-ENTITY-ID TLV from RFC 8232 may be added for such LSPs to identify the PCE that created them.
sections.eli5: Each request has a ticket number, and the router puts the same number on its reply so the helper knows which request it answers. A small checkbox says whether you are building or removing.

sections.title: Creating and Deleting an LSP
sections.content:
For creation, the LSP is set up using RSVP-TE. The PCInitiate MUST contain an LSP object with the reserved PLSP-ID 0, the SYMBOLIC-PATH-NAME TLV to correlate the PCC-assigned PLSP-ID with the LSP, and an ERO. The END-POINTS object MAY be added to state destination addresses, and the source address is either given or left for the PCC to choose by setting it to 0.0.0.0 or ::. On success the PCC MUST send a PCRpt with a non-zero PLSP-ID and the Create and Delegate flags set.

The PCC answers bad requests with a PCErr. Examples: a non-zero PLSP-ID on a create (Error-type 19, value 8), a missing ERO (type 6, value 9), a missing SYMBOLIC-PATH-NAME (type 10, value 8), a name already in use (type 23, value 1), unacceptable parameters (type 24, value 1), an internal error (type 24, value 2) and a signaling error (type 24, value 3). A PCC SHOULD be able to cap the number or resource share of PCE-initiated LSPs, and the PCE SHOULD be able to cap pending requests or wait time.

For deletion, the PCE sends a PCInitiate with the target PLSP-ID and the R flag set. A PLSP-ID of zero removes all LSPs with the C flag set that are delegated to the PCE. Unknown, undelegated or non-PCE-initiated PLSP-IDs each produce a PCErr, and after removal the PCC MUST send a PCRpt that echoes the SRP-ID-number with R set.
sections.eli5: When the helper asks for a road, it must give the road a name and a route. If the name is taken or the route makes no sense, the router says no and tells it why.

sections.title: Delegation, Cleanup and Synchronization
sections.content:
The PCC MUST delegate a PCE-initiated LSP to the PCE on instantiation and MUST NOT revoke that delegation on an active session. Every PCRpt from the PCC must keep the delegation bit at 1, and a PCE that sees 0 MUST send a PCErr (type 19, value 7) and MAY close the session.

Control can revert to the PCC if a PCE returns the delegation (for example to move an LSP between PCEs), or if the session fails and the Redelegation Timeout Interval expires. The LSP is then an orphan until the State Timeout Interval timer expires. During that time the original PCE or a backup can take it back by sending a PCInitiate with just the SRP and LSP objects and the LSP's PLSP-ID, and the PCC MUST redelegate it and stop the timer.

The timer is what keeps a PCE crash from immediately disrupting services: LSPs are cleaned up only when it expires. On expiry the behaviour follows local policy, either removing the LSP or reverting to operator-defined default parameters, and the PCC MUST support removal.

During state synchronization the PCC reports its LSPs with the SYNC flag, also setting the Create flag for PCE-initiated ones. At the end, the PCE SHOULD send a PCInitiate to create missing LSPs or remove unwanted ones, though it might hold back, for example if the PCC is slow or the operator does not want to disrupt active flows.
sections.eli5: If the helper disappears, the roads it built are not torn up at once. They stay for a while, and if a new helper shows up it can take charge of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8231 apply, and the ability to create state on a PCC adds new attack vectors.

A malicious PCE (spoofed or compromised) could flood a PCC with instantiation requests and use up network and LSR resources, or cause rapid flaps. A PCC protects itself with a limit on LSPs or resources, answering with Error-type 19, value 6 and being free to drop further PCInitiate messages. For flaps it can limit them per unit of time and answer with Error-type 19, value 10.

A malicious PCC, or one at its limit, can ignore requests and consume PCE resources since the PCE keeps state per LSP. The PCE can limit pending requests or set a timeout, and MAY close the session or remove all the LSPs it initiated.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can give orders could give too many. So the router can say that is enough, and the helper does not wait forever for a router that stays silent.
